## Part 22: what a check of the whole found (planned 2026-10-12)

The owner's twenty-second word, on 2026-10-12: that much code has been written, as professionally as could be, but like
any professional work it may hold mistakes, wrong choices or gaps; a comprehensive check of everything, then the
problems found fixed from the most important to the least.

**Status (2026-10-12): planned.** How the check was made. Four reviews read the code by area: the policy and what a run
may reach; the run's own machinery (the loop, the models, memory, the scheduler, undo); the store, the API and the
daemon's plumbing; the web UI and the desktop shell. Each finding came with the lines it rests on and a case that shows
it, and was read again in the code before it was ranked by weight: what lets a run do what the owner did not allow, or
loses data, first; a bug on a common path or a race next; an edge or a missing timeout after; the rest last. Beside the
reviews: the offline smoke suite on main (289 passed, one skipped), the history searched for keys (none but the fake
ones of the redaction tests), and the dependencies checked against the advisories (`pip-audit` over 79 packages and
`npm audit`: none; the Rust crates were not checked, `cargo audit` is not installed).

**The shape of this part (the decisions).** Five items in the order of weight, each a pull request of its own: what a
run may change, send and open (135); spending, pacing and stops when two things happen at once (136); a reply cut off
taken for an answer (137); the store and the daemon's plumbing (138); the web UI and the desktop shell (139). What would
change the design, or needs another account of the Mac to show, is left to the owner, not built. A finding that a second
reading does not bear out is not fixed. A sixth item (140) came from the final review of the five: spellings of a line
that the guards of 135 did not read.

### How to start part 22 (the handoff prompt)

> Read ROADMAP.md part 22 and the status table of part 9 (rows 135 to 140). One item at a time, in order; the protocol
> of part 5 (branch, gate, PR, Linear MYP issue, squash merge, hash in the table, log line) is unchanged. Read each
> finding again in the code before fixing it, and give each fix a test that fails on the code of before. Never touch the
> owner's data directory except to read it, by the kinds and numbers of what is stored, and to restart the daemon when
> `/api/status` shows no active run; PLAN.md stays untracked. The owner reads Turkish; everything written is English.

### 135. What a run may change, send and open

**Status: done.** Merged as `cb76e7d` (PR #169, MYP-276 Done).

**As built (2026-10-12).** `dotagent.policy.paths` gains the path class `dot`: what Dot loads and runs, and its
emergency stop (`Runtime.dot_paths`: the plugin folders with `[plugins] dirs`, `plugins-data`, the skill folders with
`[skills] dirs`, `playbooks` and `STOP`). A run reads it as it reads the home folder; the file tools and the shell guard
judge a change there as they judge one of a protected location (`secret_access`, refused outside `yolo`), with the
reason "changes what Dot loads and runs". The shell guard also learns where more commands write: a copy (`cp`, `ln`,
`install`, `ditto`, `rsync`, `scp`) reads its sources and writes its last operand, so a skill's template copied into the
workspace stays allowed; `rsync` and `scp` are judged on what they write on this Mac as well as for the other machine;
`git clone` on its folder, `curl` and `wget` on the files they save, `tar` and `unzip` on the folder they unpack into,
and an interpreter's inline code on the places of Dot's it names. A browser upload of a file from those folders keeps
the `exfiltration` flag it had. A new flag, `upload`, marks a shell line that sends data out: `curl` with a body or a
method, `git push`, `scp` and `rsync` to another machine, `ssh`, `sftp` and the sockets, a code host's command line that
creates, comments, edits, merges or deletes (`gh api` with fields or a method), and inline code that names the network,
which now counts as fetching too; it changes nothing in a run that read no untrusted content and asks in one that did.
`truncate` outside the workspace is destructive, so the default preset asks. `RunManager.delegate` gives an agent's run
the stricter of the agent's approvals and the sender's (`ask`, then `auto`, then `yolo`). `check_browser_url` refuses
this Mac on the daemon's port in any spelling a browser reads (`localhost` and the names under it, `127.1`,
`2130706433`, `[::1]`, an IPv4 address written as IPv6) and the names of `[server] reach`; the browser session, the
browser tools and the web tools use it, and a server of this Mac on another port still opens. The desktop's app role
`dot` (the shell's bundle, `dev.dot.desktop`) refuses a step in Dot's own window outside `yolo`.
`tests/smoke/test_chrome_front.py`, which changes the Mac's front application, is marked `desktop` as well. Tests: unit
tests for the shell guard (Dot's folders changed and read, sends with and without untrusted content, `truncate`), the
browser's refusal and the desktop role; smoke tests through a real runtime (the file and shell tools on a plugin's and a
skill's files), through the team (an agent set to `yolo` answering runs that ask, review and go without asking) and in
a browser (a session whose daemon listens on the test site's port); each fails on the code of before.

**What.** Dot's own folders, the ones it loads and runs, are read but never changed by a run outside `yolo`; a shell
line that sends data out asks once the run has read untrusted content; an agent answers a message in the stricter of its
approvals and the sender's; the browser never opens Dot's own interface, and the desktop tools never act in Dot's own
window outside `yolo`; truncating a file outside the workspace counts as destructive.

### 136. Spending, pacing and stops when two things happen at once

**Status: done.** Merged as `bb18c32` (PR #170, MYP-277 Done).

**As built (2026-10-12).** `dotagent.agent.gate.SiteLocks`, one per runtime (`Runtime.site_locks`) and shared by the
gates of all its runs, holds a lock per site for its pace and one for its spending: a public or social action is checked
against the pace, decided, spaced and recorded under the first; a payment with an amount on a site with caps reads what
was spent, is decided and is recorded under the second. A second run's payment or post on the same site waits for the
first, the owner's answer included, and is judged from what the first did. `RunManager.emergency_stop`, which
`POST /api/failsafe` calls, ends every active run with the result "Emergency stop: every active run was stopped." (the
ending `emergency_stop`), so the campaign of a session it ends stops instead of planning the next one; while the `STOP`
file exists the scheduler fires no schedule (a due firing is skipped to its next time with the status "skipped: the
emergency stop is engaged") and starts no campaign session. A run's task starts eagerly, so a stop that comes before its
first step lands inside it and ends it as any stop does (before, the run stayed queued, its thread refused new runs and
the daemon's shutdown waited for it forever). A takeover brings up the tab in the browser the run works in
(`loop.browser_of`: a campaign's for its sessions) and frees the run again when the tab cannot be brought up. The
scheduler reads each due schedule again just before it fires it, so one switched off or deleted meanwhile does not fire,
and a campaign stopped or marked achieved while its session was being started (the owner's Stop found no session to
stop) ends that session at once. A run whose end cannot be recorded is logged with the traceback
(`run_end_not_recorded`), its handle is freed and its waiters wake. The inbox of a run is shut the moment the run ends,
before anything awaits, so a message sent then is refused instead of being accepted and dropped. Tests: two runs paying,
and two posting, on one site at once; a session the emergency stop ends and its campaign held; a schedule skipped under
the stop; a schedule switched off during a tick; a campaign stopped while its session starts; a takeover of a campaign's
session and one whose tab cannot be brought up; a run stopped before its first step, a message sent while its end is
recorded, a store that fails to record it. Each fails on the code of before.

**What.** The spending cap and the pace of public actions are read, decided and recorded under one lock per host that
every run shares, so two runs that pay or post at the same moment cannot pass the cap or the pace together. The
emergency stop ends the runs it stops as stopped by it, and campaigns and schedules wait while it is engaged. A run
stopped before its first step is cleaned up like any other; a takeover acts on the browser its run uses and lets the run
go on when it fails; a schedule or a campaign changed while its run was being started is read again first; a run whose
end cannot be recorded says so; a message sent while a run shuts down is not lost.

### 137. A reply cut off is not an answer

**Status: done.** Merged as `43cf3f9` (PR #171, MYP-278 Done).

**As built (2026-10-12).** A reply without tool calls that the model service ended before it was complete, at its output
limit (the finish `length`: the service's own `length`, `max_tokens`, `max_output_tokens` or
`model_context_window_exceeded`) or for an abnormal reason (the finish `other`: a content filter, a refusal, a reason
the codecs do not know), is not taken as the run's answer in any mode. The loop stores a note that says how the reply
ended, in the service's own words, and asks the model to go on with its tools or to give the complete answer again in
fewer words. The note counts as a nudge: after `[agent] finish_nudges` of them in a row the run fails with "The model's
replies were cut short and the run did not finish (the last one ended with '…')." (the ending `cut_short`, "replies from
the model cut short"). An Ollama reply whose `done_reason` is empty is a normal stop, as the chat and messages codecs
already took an empty reason. Tests: a chat whose first reply is cut short ends with the complete second one; a task run
whose replies keep being cut short fails saying so; the reasons Ollama gives for a reply's end. Each fails on the code
of before.

**What.** A model's reply that ended because it ran out of room, or for any reason other than its end, is not taken as
the run's last answer: the loop asks the model to go on, or ends the run saying why.

### 138. The store and the daemon's plumbing

**Status: done.** Merged as `3f64036` (PR #172, MYP-279 Done).

**As built (2026-10-12).** Every write of the store that fails or is cancelled part way is rolled back before its error
goes on (`_writing`), so no part of it waits in an open transaction for the next writer's commit; the waits for a lock
another process holds stay as they were. Dot's own Chrome is closed when a step after its start fails or is cancelled,
instead of being left running with its profile locked until the daemon restarts. The numbers of the configuration that
would stop the daemon are refused when it is read: below 1 for the runs, the tools and the calls at once, the tries and
the tabs, 0 or less for the timeouts and the scheduler's tick, a port outside 1 to 65535. A screenshot is written to a
file of its own that then takes its name, and a file under that name whose size is not the image's is written again. The
push sender and the stream of lifecycle events listen to their own kinds only (`EventBus.subscribe_kinds`), so the live
text of busy runs no longer pushes a question or an end out of their queue, and a listener that falls behind logs it
once (`event_listener_fell_behind`). The reapers of idle tabs and terminals log a failure and go on with the others;
closing the runtime, the browser pool and the terminals tries every part and raises after (`AsyncExitStack`). A restart
gives `run_finished` to the runs it closes and to older closed runs that still have events, so a prune is not undone;
the runs are indexed by chat, by the run that delegated them and by agent, the approvals by status; the columns, the
backfill and the indexes an older database gains are one transaction. A campaign, session or schedule whose start fails
after its run was made deletes the run with the thread (`delete_threads`; `delete_thread` is gone). `POST /api/runs`
refuses `standing` with `agent_id` and `browser` without `standing` (422). An upload named like a file Dot keeps next to
it (`meta.json`, `text.txt`, in any case) gets an underscore before its name. Tests: a write stopped part way; a
screenshot left cut short; a run whose events were pruned; the indexes; the bounds; a listener of a few kinds while runs
stream; a firing whose run fails after it was made; the start requests; the upload names. Each fails on the code of
before. Not tested: the Chrome closed after a failed step (only a visible Chrome has a step there) and the transaction
of the migration.

**What.** A write of several statements that is cancelled midway leaves no transaction open; a Chrome started for a run
that is cancelled meanwhile is closed, not lost; the configuration's numbers are held to sensible bounds when it is
read; a screenshot is written whole before it is kept under its hash; a subscription that cannot keep up logs what it
drops; a reaper that dies says so, and closing the runtime goes on past a part that fails; an attachment's name never
collides with the files Dot keeps beside it. And the smaller ones: pruning that a restart could undo, indexes for the
commonest queries, a backfill that a crash could skip, a failed start that leaves a run behind, a request to start a run
whose fields contradict each other.

### 139. The web UI and the desktop shell

**Status: done.** Merged as `fcd052b` (PR #173, MYP-280 Done).

**As built (2026-10-12).** In the desktop shell, a link that the page opens in a new window (every link of a model's
answer does) goes to the default browser through `open`, and the shell opens no window for it; an address other than
`http` or `https` is refused, and no address is logged (a refused one only by its scheme), since a link can carry what
its page put in it. The shell's watcher starts from the page the shell opened, so its first look no longer loads the UI
again, and it leaves the UI for the down page after three polls in a row that the daemon left unanswered
(`MISSES_BEFORE_DOWN`) instead of after one slow answer; the first answer after that brings the UI back. A ⇧⌘Space that
another app holds no longer stops the shell: it starts without the shortcut, and the menu says so and keeps New chat.
The shell's New chat puts the cursor in the home's box again (`window.focusComposer`, which the shell calls, was never
set). In the web UI, the sidebar reads its chats and its activity again when the event stream is back after a break,
since the stream replays nothing; a fault of the page in showing one event is logged with the stream and the event and
told in a toast, at most one every ten seconds, and the stream goes on with the next event, every listener of the
lifecycle getting each one (before, the event was lost and the connection taken for broken); the home's box waits for
the models before it reads what it starts with (the list is asked once per page, as the box of a follow-up already did),
so a reasoning level kept from before is checked against the model's levels instead of being dropped; a note, a rule to
draft or a key is refused while the one before is being saved, so Enter pressed twice keeps one; the newest load of the
sidebar and of Activity answers for what they show, and Activity makes one load of an event and the refresh it starts;
an approval card on the home shows the decision at once, and a refresh that fails after it is told; an answer that is
not JSON (a proxy's page at the daemon's address) is an `ApiError` naming the path, the status and the start of the
answer. The CI's jobs get a token that can only read the repository (`permissions: contents: read`). Tests: in a
browser, a note sent twice from the keyboard before the first save is answered is sent once and kept once, and an answer
that is not JSON is an error naming its path; each fails on the code of before. The shell's changes are checked by
`cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy -D warnings`; the app is rebuilt by the owner. Left to the owner: the CI's actions
pinned by commit rather than by tag, and the shell's capability narrowed to the daemon's port.

**What.** In the desktop app a link that opens a new window opens in the browser; the shell's watcher neither reloads
the page at its first look nor sends it to the down page after one slow answer, and a shortcut it cannot register no
longer stops it; the sidebar reads the chats again after the stream reconnects; an error in handling one event is shown,
not taken for a lost connection; the home's box keeps the reasoning level chosen before the models load; a note, a rule
or a key is never added twice by a key pressed twice. And the smaller ones: answers that arrive out of order, an
approval card left after a failed refresh, the shell's New chat, an answer that is not JSON, and the rights of the CI's
token.

### 140. The gaps the final review found in the guards

**Status: done.** Merged as `25da5f2` (PR #174, MYP-281 Done).

**As built (2026-10-12).** The shell guard reads more of a line. A copy or a move given the folder it writes into by an
option (`-t`, `--target-directory`, GNU's spellings) writes that folder, so one into Dot's own folders is refused
outside `yolo` and one out of them into the workspace is allowed (before, the first was judged a change of the home
folder and the second was refused). `dd` is judged on the file it writes (`of=`) and on a protected one it reads
(`if=`). A git command other than a read, run in one of Dot's own folders (by `cd` or `-C`), changes what Dot loads and
runs. perl and ruby with `-i` write the files they are given, and the words of switches of perl, ruby, python, node and
php are read letter by letter (`_Switches`), so the code of `-pe 'code'`, `-ne`, `-Bc` or `--eval=` is inline code that
the checks for the network and for Dot's folders read. A line sends data out also when curl has `-d`, `-F` or `-T` in a
word of switches, `-XPOST`, `--request=PUT`, `--json` or `--form-string`, wget `--post-data`, `--post-file`,
`--body-data`, `--body-file` or a method that changes something, httpie and xh a form, such a method or a data item, and
when inline code runs a command of the network or uses a mail or file transfer library; curl's `-sSfL` and `-X GET`,
wget's `-T` (a timeout, which counted as an upload before) and httpie's query and header items do not. The browser reads
a dot at the end of a host as none, so `127.0.0.1.` on the daemon's port is Dot's own interface. Tests: the new
spellings in the unit tests of the shell guard (Dot's folders changed and read, sends and reads after untrusted content,
a protected read, everyday lines) and of the browser's refusal; thirty fail on the code of before. Left as they are, and
said in the README: the guard reads the line, not what a program does, so a script a run writes and then runs, or code
that builds the path it writes, is judged as running a script; a name that resolves to this Mac is another origin, where
the page has no token. Keeping those folders out of the shell's reach would need a sandbox for the shell's commands,
left to the owner.

**What.** The spellings the final review of the five items found in the guards of 135: a copy's target folder option,
`dd`, git in Dot's own folders, files edited in place and code in a word of switches, more ways curl, wget, httpie and
inline code send data out, and a loopback address with a dot at its end.

### 141. The commands of a run are kept out of Dot's own files by macOS

**Status: done.** Merged as `6fe0263` (PR #176, MYP-282 Done).

**As built (2026-10-12).** `dotagent.policy.sandbox` builds two profiles of the macOS sandbox (`sandbox-exec`):
everything is allowed but reading or changing Dot's guarded files (its key file, token, push key, configuration,
database, browser profile, the data directory of the owner's Chrome and the journals of `dotx undo`), changing what it
loads and runs (`Runtime.dot_paths`), and renaming or removing a folder above any of them; the profile of the search
tools refuses reading the owner's protected locations as well. Outside `yolo` (`run_sandbox`), the shell tool, a
terminal session, the AppleScript tool (with what it runs by `do shell script`) and the search tools' ripgrep start in
it; the processes of a yolo run start as before, since the guard lets such a run change Dot's own files too, and a
terminal session a yolo run opened takes no line from a run that is not one. The daemon checks at its start that
`sandbox-exec` runs both profiles and stops with a configuration error when it does not; `[shell] sandbox = false` turns
the sandbox off. Probed on macOS 26.6 before it was built: the sandbox refuses a read or a write through a script, a
symbolic link, a hard link, a rename out, another letter case and the firmlink of the data volume, and the rename of a
folder above, while a file can still be made inside that folder; starting in it costs no measurable time. What it costs:
macOS starts no program that runs as root inside a sandbox (`ps`, `top`, `sudo`, `crontab`), which the description of
the shell tool tells the model (`pgrep -lf`, `lsof`). What it does not cover, said in the README: a program a command
has act for it (Terminal through `open`, a launchd job, an application driven by Apple Events). Tests: smoke tests
through a real runtime (a script that reads the token, a skill planted, the settings changed, the emergency stop's file
made, a hard link, the data folder moved; a search of the data folder and of a protected location; a terminal session;
an AppleScript), the four of which fail on the code of before; unit tests for the text of a profile and for a process
held to it.

**What.** The processes a run starts outside `yolo` (shell commands, terminal sessions, AppleScript, the search tools)
run in a macOS sandbox that keeps them out of Dot's own files, whatever program does it, so what the shell guard cannot
read (a script the run wrote, code that builds a path) no longer reaches them.

### 142. What the guards of the desktop and of the shell see

**Status: done.** Merged as `d765da9` (PR #177, MYP-283 Done).

**As built (2026-10-12).** The desktop: `window_role` takes a window of any application but the terminals, Finder,
System Settings, the messengers and the password managers for Dot's own when its title is the one Dot's web UI gives its
page (`Dot`, `<page> · Dot`, with `(2) ` in front while two things wait for the owner), as a browser shows it, with its
own name or the profile's after a dash; a page of another site that takes such a title is refused as well. The title is
read at each step from the window it acts in: the one the control is in, the one under the point (as the window server
names it), else the focused window of the application (`ax.window_of`, `ax.title_of`). A step there is judged as one in
the desktop app, refused outside `yolo` by the review of each step as it runs. Probed on this Mac: Chrome's
accessibility title is the page's title and then a dash and more, while the window server gives the page's title alone.
The shell: a line that replaces a file that is there outside the workspace and the temporary folders is destructive
(`_replaced_by`, `_replacing`): a redirect that empties it (`>`, `>|`, `&>`), a copy or a move onto it or into a folder
that holds a file of its name (`cp -n` and `mv -n` keep it), `install`, `ditto`, `ln -f`, `tee` without `-a`, `dd`
without `conv=notrunc`; so the default preset, which asks before destroying something outside the workspace, asks. A
file made anew, an append and a change inside the workspace or the temporary folders do not ask. Tests: unit tests of
the window's role (Dot's titles in four browsers and an unknown one; titles that only look alike; a terminal and Finder)
and of the lines that replace a file and those that keep it; on the code of before every browser window had the role of
its application and the lines that replace a file were allowed. Not run here: the desktop steps themselves, whose tests
move the pointer (the owner's to run).

**What.** The desktop tools take a window of a browser that shows Dot's own interface for Dot's own window, so a step
there is refused outside `yolo` as one in the desktop app is. A line that replaces a file that exists outside the
workspace (a redirect that does not append, a copy or a move onto it, `tee` without `-a`, `dd`) is destructive, as
removing it is, so the presets that ask before destroying something outside the workspace ask.

### 143. The token goes only to the daemon

**Status: done.** Merged as `57180ea` (PR #178, MYP-284 Done).

**As built (2026-10-12).** The daemon answers `GET /api/proof?nonce=<32 to 128 hex digits>` without the token with
`daemon_proof`: an HMAC-SHA256 keyed with the token over a fixed label and the nonce, in hex, which only a holder of the
token can give. Every client checks it with a fresh nonce of its own before it sends the token. The command line
(`prove_daemon`), before `dotx open` and `dotx url` give the signed-in address and before `dotx service permissions`
posts: any other answer stops it, and it names `lsof` for what listens on the port. The desktop shell (`look`), at each
poll before it asks for the count with the token and so before it opens the UI with the token in the address; its menu
bar item says that something else answers at the daemon's address. It uses the `hmac` crate (new to its lock) with
`sha2`, `hex` and `getrandom`, which its lock already had. The web UI (`proven` in `api.js`), before each request,
stream and image it sends with the token; requests made while a proof is on its way share it, and a proof that has
settled serves no later request. In the page an answer with another proof is told as a refused token (the page asks for
one) and any other answer as a daemon that cannot be reached; Web Crypto is there on the loopback address in WebKit and
in Chromium (probed). Left: a page that another program served at the daemon's address reads what the browser keeps for
that address, the token among it. Tests: the proof of a known token and nonce, held by the Python and the Rust tests
alike; the route, open without the token, refusing what is not a nonce; the command line against a real program on a
free port that answers the health check as the daemon does but not the proof, or asks for the token as the daemon of
before does (no token sent, no address given), and against the real daemon; the page against such an answer (no request
carries the token, the page asks for one) and then against the daemon; the shell over real sockets against the daemon,
another program, a program without the proof and nothing at all. Each failed on the code of before (the shell's with its
poll made the old way, which sent the token to the other program). CI's desktop job runs `cargo test` too. The shell's
part reaches the owner's Mac when the owner rebuilds the desktop app.

**What.** Before the command line, the desktop shell and the web UI's reconnection send the API token, the daemon proves
that it holds it (a keyed hash of a fresh nonce), so a program that holds the daemon's port while the daemon is down is
not given the token.

### 144. The records of a run and the emergency stop

**Status: done.** Merged as `c17da1a` (PR #179, MYP-285 Done).

**As built (2026-10-12).** Every process that drives runs (the daemon, `dotx run`) takes an owner with its first run: a
lock file under `run-owners/` that it holds with `flock` while it lives and that no program it starts inherits, so the
system lets go of it when the process ends, however it ends (`agent/owners.py`). A run records its owner (a new `owner`
column). A daemon that starts closes as cut off only the active runs whose owner no process holds any more, and those of
before the column; it expires only the approvals of runs no longer active, and deletes the lock files nobody holds. The
sandbox of a run's commands keeps them out of `run-owners/`. The emergency stop counts its stops: a run being launched
when one comes, which it could not find, ends as an emergency stop once it is registered; a campaign's session that
started while the `STOP` file appeared ends so, and its campaign stops; the scheduler looks for the file again after it
started the run of a schedule, and before each campaign whose session is due. The smaller findings: the record of a
learned skill (`playbook.json`) and its `SKILL.md` are written whole (`core/files.py`, shared with the themes), and
every change of the playbooks holds a lock file in their folder, so runs that end at once lose no count; a note saved
twice at once stays one (`add_memory_once`, one `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction); a call of a group of read-only calls
that fails outside its tool cancels the others and waits for them; the store's docstring says how its writes take turns;
the refresh of the notes' search index when a store opens is one `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction, so a note another
process adds meanwhile stays in the index; only the messages that name screenshots take the places of the screenshots
read back; `dotx.log` is moved to `dotx.log.1` at 10 MB, and a process whose file was moved or deleted writes its next
line to the new one; a launch of Dot's own Chrome given up while Chrome starts closes that Chrome once it is up, so the
profile stays free; the browser's page size (320 by 240 to 3840 by 2160), its screenshot quality (1 to 100) and its
viewport margin (0 or more) are checked when the configuration is read; and the page says a stream is live only once the
server has taken it. Tests: owners held by real child processes, one killed and one that left a program running; the
store closing only the runs of owners that are gone, with their approvals; a child process driving a run that a starting
daemon leaves while the child lives and closes once it is killed; the emergency stop while a session's brief is written
(of two due campaigns the second starts no session), while a run is launched, and while the run of a schedule is
started; eight threads counting uses of one playbook beside a listing; two saves of one note at once with a slow
embedder; a group whose first call fails while the second waits; a second connection that holds a note while a store
opens; a call whose arguments name a `file`; the log rotated by its size and by another process; a launch of a real
headless Chrome given up once Chrome holds its profile; the new bounds; and a page following a stream that is not
answered and one that is. Each failed on the code of before; the scheduler's part of the emergency stop also failed with
the manager's part in place but not its own.

**What.** A daemon that starts does not close the records of a run that `dotx run` drives in a process of its own; a run
that starts as the emergency stop is engaged ends at once; and the smaller findings of part 22 that a second reading
bears out are fixed.

**Status: done.** Merged as `969d5f0` (PR #180, MYP-286 Done).

**As built (2026-10-12).** Every action of the CI's two jobs is pinned by the commit its tag named when it was pinned,

which one is refused (the gates of its runs share the runtime's site locks, which hold each site's spending lock too;

**What.** The actions of the CI pinned by their commit; the desktop shell's window allowed to talk to the app only from

### 146. The gaps the final review of part 23 found

**Status: done.** Merged as `e558f21` (PR #181, MYP-287 Done).

**As built (2026-10-12).** What Dot runs at its start is kept from a run's commands. Dot's own code joins what it loads
and runs (`_own_code` in `runtime.py`): the folder its package is imported from, the Python environment it runs in
(`sys.prefix`), the Python under that (`sys.base_prefix`) and the file of the launchd job, so outside `yolo` the file
tools, the shell guard and the sandbox keep a run from changing them, as they keep it from its plugins and skills. The
launchd job starts Python with `-P`: its working directory is Dot's home, where a command of a run may make files, and
`python -m` put that directory first on the path Python imports from. The login shell whose environment Dot reads at its
start runs its startup files in the sandbox of a run's commands (`read_login_env` takes the words of a sandbox), so what
a command put in them reaches no further at Dot's start than the command could. A search that meets places it may not
read (the sandbox's, or a file's permissions) shows what it found elsewhere and names those places, where ripgrep's
error made the whole search fail before; any other error of ripgrep still fails it. The shell guard reads zsh's
redirects past noclobber, spelt with `!` or `|` (`>!`, `>>!`, `&>!`, `&>|`, `>&!`, `>&|`, `&>>|`, `>>&`, `>>&!`):
before, the `!` was taken for the file and the `|` for a pipe, so the file the line writes went unseen. A run that read
a playbook another run has just retired, or the owner deleted, counts nothing and goes on to distil its own (the check
is made under the lock). Said in the README, not built: a key kept in the keychain is read by a command through
`security`, in the sandbox too (the key file is sealed; keeping `security` out of the sandbox would break the
command-line tools that keep their own tokens in the keychain), and the programs Dot starts itself (its browser, the MCP
servers) and the owner's shell run from where they are installed, which a command may change under the owner's account.
Tests: a command that writes into Dot's package and into its environment, refused; the base Python and the job's file
among what Dot loads and runs; a search and a file listing over Dot's home that show a match beside its sealed files
with a note of what they did not read; a startup file of the login shell that reads Dot's token, refused at Dot's start;
the job's words, run in a folder holding a package named `dotagent`, which run the installed Dot; eleven zsh spellings
that change Dot's folders and three that replace a file outside the workspace; a use counted after the playbook was
retired. Each failed on the code of before (fifteen unit tests and three smoke tests).

**What.** The gaps the final review of the five items found, each read again in the code: what Dot runs at its start
(its own code, the login shell, and the working directory of the launchd job, found on the way), a search that meets a
place it may not read, zsh's spellings of a redirect past noclobber, and a playbook retired while a run ended; and what
the sandbox does not cover, said in the README.

**As built (2026-10-13).** A search (`search_files`, `find_files`) that meets a folder whose reading macOS broke off
shows what it found elsewhere and names that folder in its note of what it did not read, as item 146 made it do for the

## Part 24: the queue of a chat, after T3 Code (planned 2026-10-13)

The owner's twenty-fourth word, on 2026-10-13, after part 23: add T3 Code's queued messages to Dot, as T3 Code has them.

**Status (2026-10-13): planned.** T3 Code's queue was read in its source (the banner above its composer, and the
server's rules for when a queued message starts and when it waits), then Dot's run page, run manager and store for where
a queue fits.

**The shape of this part (the decisions).** One item (148). The queue is the daemon's, kept per chat in the store, so it
goes on with no page open, and a queued message is not a run until it starts: a run in the `queued` status would count
as working, be closed at a restart and keep the daemon from being idle. It starts when the chat's run ends done and
waits on any other end, as in T3 Code: a stop, a failure or a restart holds the queue until the owner resumes it.

### How to start part 24 (the handoff prompt)

> Read ROADMAP.md part 24 and the status table of part 9 (row 148). The protocol of part 5 (branch, gate, PR, Linear MYP
> issue when the connector is signed in, squash merge, hash in the table, log line) is unchanged. Give the change tests
> that fail on the code of before, and check the page in a browser, wide and on a phone, light and dark. Never touch the
> owner's data directory except to read it, by the kinds and numbers of what is stored, and to restart the daemon when
> `/api/status` shows no active run; PLAN.md stays untracked. The owner reads Turkish; everything written is English.

### 148. The queue of a chat, after T3 Code

**Status: done.** Merged as `5f6747b` (PR #184; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** A message sent on a chat's page while its run works waits in the chat's queue, which the
daemon keeps (`queued_messages` in the store, a row per message in its place, with the mode, model, reasoning,
approvals, goal mode, agent and files it was sent with; `queue_holds` for a held queue). When a run of the chat ends
done, the run manager starts the queue's first message as the chat's next run, with those choices, and takes it out; the
next one waits for that run, and so on. Any other end, a stop, a failure or a start of the daemon, holds the queue until
the owner resumes it: what failed would likely fail the next message too, and a stop stops the chat. Nothing starts
while a run of the chat works, a delegated run or a campaign's session leaves the queue alone, and a campaign's chat
takes no queue, so a message there steers the session as before. The page shows the queue above the composer as T3 Code
does (`static/js/queue.js`): a sheet whose head (an ordered list, Queued, the count, a chevron) folds it, and a row per
message: a handle that drags it to another place or moves it with the arrow keys, its text on one line with all of it in
the tooltip, a pencil that edits it in the composer (the send says Save; Escape or Cancel gives the box its draft back),
Steer, which sends it to the run at work now, and × to take it out. While the run works the send says Queue; ⌘⇧Enter
steers the run with what the box holds, past the queue, or with the queue's next message when the box is empty. A held
queue says it is paused, with Resume. Each change is a `queue_changed` event of the lifecycle stream, so every open page
shows the queue as it is, and the page of the run that ended follows the chat to the run its queue started. The API:
`GET|POST|PUT /api/threads/{id}/queue`, `POST /api/threads/{id}/queue/resume`, `PATCH|DELETE /api/queue/{id}` and
`POST /api/queue/{id}/steer`. Found by the browser test and fixed before the merge: the rows were drawn anew on every
change, which took the focus from a handle moved with the arrow keys and broke a drag as it began, and on a phone Cancel
was cut to the width of an icon. Tests: messages queued while a run works start one after the other once the run before
has ended done, with their choices; a stopped run and a failed run hold the queue, which Resume starts; a queued message
steered reaches the run and leaves the queue; the order and the text the owner gives are kept, an order that does not
name each message once is refused, and a start of the daemon holds the queue; the page, wide and on a phone, light and
dark: three messages queued, one moved with the keys and one by a drag, one edited, the sheet folded, one steered with
its button and one with the key, the chat followed to the next run, which is stopped, and the paused queue resumed. They
failed on the code of before, where the run manager has no queue and the send says Steer.

**What.** T3 Code's queued messages in Dot: a message sent while a run works waits and starts after it, instead of
steering the run at once, and the queue can be reordered, edited, sent into the run and resumed, from any open page.
