### 149. The scheduler goes on past a failure

**Status: done.** Merged as `1ec1497` (PR #186; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** `Scheduler.tick` does its three parts (the due schedules, the due sessions of campaigns, the
reflection's check) each on its own: a part that fails is logged with its error (`scheduler_part_failed`) and holds up
neither of the others, and the failures are raised together at the end of the tick, as an `ExceptionGroup`. The loop
tries a failed tick again at the next one and counts the failed ticks in a row; at `FAILED_TICKS_TO_END` (20, five
minutes at the default `tick_s` of 15 seconds) it ends with the last tick's failures, and the daemon with it, as before,
so schedules never stop firing unseen, and the service's job starts the daemon again. Before, the first error that the
tick did not catch (the store failing as it listed the due schedules or campaigns, a campaign's start failing with an
error that is not Dot's own, the reflection's check) ended the loop, the daemon and every run it held. Tests: a listing
of the due campaigns that fails once, after which the loop goes on ticking; one that fails every time, which ends the
loop after twenty ticks with the store's error. Both failed on the code of before, where the first failure ended the
loop.

**What.** A tick of the scheduler that fails, in the store, a campaign's start or the reflection's check, is logged and
tried again at the next tick, and the other parts of the tick go on; only a failure that lasts many ticks in a row ends
the scheduler and the daemon. Before, one error that the tick did not catch ended the scheduler's loop, and with it the
daemon and every run it held.

### 150. A tool that raises fails its call, not its run

**Status: done.** Merged as `ba4f2a6` (PR #187; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** The executor turns any error of a tool into a failed result of that call (`_run_checked`): an
error no tool expects, a fault in Dot rather than in what the call asked, is logged with its traceback (`tool_crashed`)
and the model reads its kind and its words; a stop of the run and the emergency stop still end it. Before, only Dot's
own errors, timeouts and the system's were caught, and any other error, such as the `UnicodeDecodeError` of `edit_file`
on a file that is not UTF-8, ended the run as an internal error. `edit_file` reads the file's bytes and changes the text
it is given and nothing else: a file that breaks every line with CRLF keeps them, and the old and the new text are taken
with CRLF too (`read_file` shows the lines without it), where before the whole file was written back with LF; a file
that is not UTF-8 text is refused, saying so, for the shell to change, rather than guessed at. Tests (scripted runs): a
tool that raises a `ValueError`, whose call fails with its kind and words while the run ends done; an edit of a CRLF
file that keeps every line end; an edit of a Latin-1 file that fails saying so and leaves the file as it was. Each
failed on the code of before.

**What.** Any error a tool raises fails that call, with the error's kind and words for the model to read, and the run
goes on; `edit_file` keeps a file's Windows line ends and refuses a file that is not UTF-8 text, saying so, where it
used to end the run.

### 151. A question a run left reaches the owner

**Status: done.** Merged as `6788a66` (PR #188; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** The phone's pushes and the page's desktop notifications (`attention.js`, which the desktop
app's notifications go through too) say the same things in the same words. A question a run left (`question_left`: a
`yolo`, scheduled or campaign run goes on without the answer) is told as one asked is; before, only `approval_requested`
and `run_finished` were, so the question waited unseen, for a campaign up to `campaign_wait_hours`. The end of a run
tells the first line of its answer rather than its goal. Three live events are new. `campaign_ended`, on the session's
run, when the goal checker accepts a campaign's outcome or the emergency stop or `campaign_max_sessions` stops it; the
owner's own Stop, Go on and Mark achieved tell nothing, and the accepted claim's banner of macOS Notification Center
went, as it would be a second one on the Mac. `schedule_missed`, of Dot itself (`SYSTEM_RUN_ID`), when a firing is
skipped as overdue or its run cannot start, once while the schedule's status stays the same; the skips of the emergency
stop and of a run still going are not told, as the owner sees those already. `daemon_restarted`, when a start finds
`<home>/daemon.running`, the mark a daemon leaves while it runs and removes only when it ends without an error, with the
number of runs that start closed. The daemon opens the push subscription before its start's own work, so the restart and
the missed firings of the first tick are pushed. Tests: a `yolo` run's question reaches the push service and the run
goes on (two posts, not one); the page tells the question, the first line of the end, a campaign's stop and a missed
firing; the scheduler tells an overdue firing and a failed start once; a campaign's accepted claim and its emergency
stop send `campaign_ended`; a real daemon that starts where one did not end cleanly pushes the restart, and takes its
own mark away when it stops; the mark stays after a daemon that raised; unit tests give the words of every message. Each
part's test failed with that part of before.

**What.** A question a run left for the owner reaches the owner as an approval does, on the phone and in the page's
notifications, and so do the ends the owner would not otherwise see: a campaign that ended by itself, a firing a
schedule missed, and (on the phone, as no page is there yet) a start of the daemon after it did not stop cleanly. The
end of a run tells the first line of its answer.

### 152. A late one-time schedule is never dropped unseen

**Status: done.** Merged as `c1ccf7e` (PR #189; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** A one-time schedule has no next time, so a skipped firing used to switch it off for good:
overdue by more than `misfire_grace_s` (the daemon was off, the Mac slept) or due while the emergency stop was engaged.
`Scheduler._fire` now treats it apart from a repeating one. Overdue, it fires late, and its run's goal begins with when
it was due and when it starts (`late_goal`), so the run can judge what the delay changes, and the owner reads it on the
run's page; within the grace it fires as before. Due while the emergency stop is engaged, it stays due with the status
`waiting: the emergency stop is engaged` (written once, not at every tick) and fires at the first tick after the
release. A repeating schedule still skips such a firing to its next time, an overdue one told to the owner since item
151. Tests (a run manager that records the goal of each start): an overdue one-time schedule starts once with the note
of its delay and is used up; one due under the emergency stop starts nothing while the stop is engaged, stays due, and
starts once after the release. Both failed on the code of before, which switched the schedule off.

**What.** A one-time schedule whose moment passed while the Mac slept or the daemon was off is never switched off: it
fires late, its run reading first when it was due; one due while the emergency stop is engaged waits for the release.

### 153. A server of tools that cannot start does not stop the daemon

**Status: done.** Merged as `a872136` (PR #190; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** `open_hub` used to stop every server again and raise when one enabled server could not start,
so `open_runtime` failed and the daemon did not start at all. Now each server that cannot start is left out with the
reason (`McpFailure`: the server, the error, its context and the server's log file; logged as `mcp_server_left_out`, or
`mcp_server_crashed` with the traceback for an error that is not one of Dot's own), the others serve their tools, and
`McpHub.failures` keeps the record. Only a cancellation still stops every server again. The check that two tools would
share a name moved into the start of each server: a server's name has no `_`, so tools of two servers never share one,
and a clash among one server's tools leaves that server out, as a wrong `allow` list does (`dotx mcp list` now shows it
too). Where it shows: `/api/status` has `mcp_failures`, and Settings › System names each server left out with the
reason; `dotx run`, `dotx resume` and `dotx chat` print a line per server before they begin; `dotx doctor`, which starts
nothing, warns (no longer fails) of a missing command or secret, and none of its MCP rows is required any more. A server
left out is tried again when Dot starts again. Tests (`tests/smoke/test_mcp.py`): the hub tests read the failure the hub
kept instead of catching the error; one good and one broken server give the good one's tools, which answer a call; a
server whose tools would share a name is left out and its process ends; `dotx run` with a broken server names it before
it begins; a real daemon with a broken and a good server starts, and its status names the broken one with the reason.
All of them failed on the code of before (the daemon ended with code 2 while it started).

**What.** An MCP server that cannot start leaves the daemon starting without its tools, and shows as broken in
`dotx doctor` and the web UI.

### 154. The memory keeps what it learns

**Status: done.** Merged as `f53eb00` (PR #191; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** Four faults of the memory, each seen in the code first. (1) The nightly merge paired a
resting lesson with a new one that said the same and gave the newer both notes' tags, so a lesson learnt again took the
`rest` tag the same night; it also paired the lessons of two agents, so one agent lost its lesson to the other's.
`duplicate_pairs` now leaves resting notes out and pairs only notes of the same agent. (2) `do`, `don` and `not` are no
search terms (the search needs that), so "Use --force with X" and "Do not use --force with X" had the same terms and the
correction was dropped as a repeat, and their embeddings are close too. `same_way_round` now keeps apart a text that
says not to (`not`, `no`, `never`, `cannot`, `n't`, the Turkish `değil`, `yok`, `asla`, `hiç`, `hiçbir`) and one that
does not: such a pair never repeats in `repeats`, a saved note that says the opposite never counts as already saying a
lesson being drawn, by words or by meaning, and such a pair never merges at night. The Turkish suffix `-ma`/`-me` is not
recognised. (3) A run's starting notes came from one budget filled group after group: the standing notes, every note the
owner wrote, the agent's lessons, then the other notes that fit, so forty notes of the owner left no room for a lesson.
The owner's notes still reach every run, as they did on purpose (they are the owner's own words), but `fit_groups` now
gives each of the four groups a quarter of the budget first, then what is left, in the same order; no relevance bar was
put on the owner's notes, as first planned, since that would undo that choice. (4) The lessons of a failed or stopped
run, drawn by the nightly reflection, were asked for with instructions that said the run reached its goal. `LessonCase`
and `LessonRequest` carry `reached_goal`, and such a run's instructions say it did not reach its goal; for both, a
lesson may say what does not work, as the digest shows. Tests: in `tests/unit/test_reflection.py`, a resting note and
another agent's note make no pair, and a lesson and the one that says not to do it make no pair, by words or by
identical embeddings; in `tests/unit/test_lessons.py`, such pairs do not repeat, in English and in Turkish, and a saved
note found with a similarity of 0.99 does not already say the opposite; in `tests/smoke/test_memory.py`, a lesson that
fits the goal reaches a run next to forty notes of the owner, part of which come along; in
`tests/smoke/test_reflection.py`, the failed and the stopped run are asked about in words that say they did not reach
their goal. All of them failed on the code of before.

**What.** The nightly merge leaves resting notes and other agents' notes alone; a lesson that says not to do something
is not taken for a repeat of the one that says to do it; each group of notes has its own share of the budget, so the
owner's notes, which reach every run, do not crowd out the agent's lessons; a lesson of a run that failed is drawn with
words that say it failed.

### 155. The compaction keeps a tail measured in tokens

**Status: done.** Merged as `5b0b2cb` (PR #192; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** A compaction kept about eight messages, whatever the budget: `split_for_summary` took a count
of messages to keep (8, from the loop; a few more when the cut fell inside a tool exchange) and the room in tokens could
only lower it, while the README and the comment on `_COMPACTION_ROOM` say that the newest messages that fit are kept.
With the default budget of 96 000 tokens that room is about 50 000 tokens less the system prompt and the tool
definitions, and a run kept about its last eight messages of it and lost the rest to the summary.
`split_for_summary(messages, max_tail_tokens)` now keeps the newest messages that come to at most the room, however many
they are: the earliest cut whose tail fits (a binary search, since the estimate only falls as the cut moves on), moved
on past tool results so that no tool exchange is cut in two, and never later than the newest assistant message, so the
newest exchange is always kept. The count (`_SUMMARY_KEEP_TAIL`) is gone. Right after a compaction the prompt is now
fuller, up to 85 % of the size at which it compacts, so a long run compacts more often than before, each time with less
to summarise; the room for the steps after it is at least the 15 % of `_COMPACTION_ROOM`. Tests: in
`tests/unit/test_continuity.py`, twenty exchanges that fit the room are all kept, and room for a tool result but not for
its call keeps neither; the case that pinned a count of three went with the count. With the old split and the loop's
count of eight, the new case failed (8 of 41 messages kept). The README sentence on what a compaction keeps now names
the size the 85 % is of.

**What.** A compaction keeps as many of the newest messages as fit in a share of the budget measured in tokens, and
never less than the newest exchange, as the README says, not about eight messages whatever the budget.

### 156. The page text of the browser and the desktop has a floor

**Status: done.** Merged as `6ad598f` (PR #193; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** The browser's tools gave the text of a page what one tool result of the run may carry less
3500 characters for the rest of the result (steps, tabs, notes and the fence lines), and the desktop's snapshot the same
of `tool_output_chars`. A run's results shrink with a small model window (never below 2000 characters), so nothing was
left for the text: a model whose window holds 32 768 tokens gets results of 3072 characters and a page body of -428, and
`browser_open` said "(empty page)". `browser_read_text` cut the text at a negative length, which in Python keeps all of
it but its end, so it handed back 6459 of 6887 characters in a result of 3072, which the executor then cut in the
middle, and it named an offset to go on from that skipped what was cut. `text_room` in `tools/base.py` now gives the
text what is left next to the rest of the result, and never less than half the result; the page body and
`browser_read_text` of the browser, and the snapshot and `desktop_read` of the desktop, use it. This changes only
results under 7000 characters (a window under about 75 000 tokens); with the default budget a page body and a window
keep 8500 characters. Tests: `tests/smoke/test_page_room.py` opens a page of eighty paragraphs on a real headless Chrome
in a run whose results are 3072 characters: the page comes back shortened within one result, with its first paragraph
and the note of how many lines are not shown, and its text is read in pages that fit, the second going on where the
first stopped; in `tests/unit/test_scaffold.py`, the desktop's snapshot budget is 1500 for a `tool_output_chars` of 3000
and stays 8500 by default. All of them failed on the code of before (the empty page, a result of 6624 characters, a
budget of -500). The desktop's snapshot still does not follow the window: it is sized from `tool_output_chars` when Dot
starts, and the executor cuts the middle out of a snapshot over a small window's result, as before.

**What.** In a small model window the text of a page has a floor: a page never comes back empty because the window is
small.

### 157. The changed notes a running run is handed, and their dates and authors

**Status: done.** Merged as `3593f6a` (PR #194; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** Two findings of the review on the memory (B8 and B9), each read again in the code first. (1)
At every step a run was handed every note changed since the step before that it had not saved itself
(`memories_changed_since`): other agents' lessons, retired notes, and as many notes as had changed, past the budget of
its starting notes. `live_memories` now hands it what it would be handed at its start: the notes it may be handed
(`visible_to`) that do not rest (`resting`), as many as fit the budget of its starting notes (`memory_budget`), and the
run is told how many more changed (`memory_search` finds them). (2) `set_memory_tags` moved a note's `updated_at`, so
the nightly `rest` and merged tags made old notes changed for every running run, and newer than their corrections under
the prompt's rule that the newer of two notes wins; a retag now leaves `updated_at`. (3) `memory_update` kept a note's
author, so a note of the owner that the model rewrote still read "the user wrote it". `rewrite_memory_note` makes the
run its author, while the owner's own edit (`PATCH /api/memories/{id}`) keeps it. The old text of a rewritten note is
not kept: the review's proposal to invalidate a note instead of overwriting it is a larger change and is not made here.
Tests: `tests/smoke/test_live_notes.py` runs a scripted model while notes change under it (an old lesson is retired,
another agent's lesson retagged, that agent learns a new lesson, the owner writes a note and another run saves forty):
the next step is handed the owner's note and part of the forty with the count of the rest, nothing of the other agent's,
and the retired lesson keeps its date. In `tests/smoke/test_memory.py`, a note of the owner that a run rewrites with
`memory_update` is the run's and reads "you saved it". Both failed on the code of before (the other agent's new lesson
was handed on; the rewritten note read "the user wrote it"), and the first failed again with each of its other two fixes
taken back alone (a retag moving the date; no budget).

**What.** A running run is handed the notes changed while it works that it would be handed at its start: not another
agent's lessons nor resting notes, and no more than the budget of its starting notes. A change of tags is no change and
leaves a note's date. A note a run rewrites becomes the run's, so the model's words never pass for the owner's.

## Part 26: continue where it left off (planned 2026-10-13)

The owner's twenty-sixth word, on 2026-10-13, while part 25 was under way: when a connection drops, or the app is closed
and opened again, Dot should go on from where it was; build that reconnection where it is missing. The same word asked
for an agent that looks for the help its Mac offers (MCP servers, skills) before it takes the hard way: part 27, planned
after this one.

**Status (2026-10-13): planned.** Each kind of break was read in the code first. What exists: the desktop app only shows
the daemon's pages, so closing it leaves the daemon and its runs at work, and opened again it shows each run from its
first event; a run's page that loses its connection follows its run again from the last event it had; a model's
connector tries a call again when retrying can get past its failure, six times in some fifteen to thirty seconds; a run
cut by a stop or a crash of the daemon can be resumed, by `dotx resume` or from its page, and with `resume = "safe"` in
`[agent]` the daemon resumes by itself, when it starts, a run it cut that was started from a page and whose cut calls
only read. What is missing: a model out of reach past its connector's tries fails the run, and a failed run cannot be
resumed; a stop of the daemon cancels its runs and waits for them to end without a bound, so a run slow to end keeps the
daemon past the thirty seconds launchd gives it before it kills it, and the stop becomes a crash, while a step cut part
way keeps none of the results of its calls that had ended; the stream of the lifecycle (`/api/stream`) replays nothing
after a break, and of the pages only the sidebar reads its lists again; every chat's queue is held when the daemon
starts, after a clean stop too; a run of `dotx run` whose terminal closes ends as stopped by the owner, which cannot be
resumed.

**The shape of this part (the decisions).** Five items in the order of weight, each a pull request of its own: a model
out of reach does not fail a run (158); a stop of the daemon is never a crash (159); pages catch up after a break (160);
a chat's queue goes on after a clean restart (161); a run whose terminal closed can be resumed (162). A run waits for
its own model rather than moving to a standby one, which takes over only for a quota, a rate limit or a key. The default
of `resume` stays `off` until evals show that `safe` helps, as its comment in the defaults says.

### How to start part 26 (the handoff prompt)

> Read ROADMAP.md part 26 and the status table of part 9 (rows 158 to 162). One item at a time, in order; the protocol
> of part 5 (branch, gate, PR, Linear MYP issue when the connector is signed in, squash merge, hash in the table, log
> line) is unchanged. Read each gap again in the code before closing it, give each change a test that fails on the code
> of before, and check a page that changes in a browser, wide and on a phone, light and dark. Never touch the owner's
> data directory except to read it, by the kinds and numbers of what is stored, and to restart the daemon when
> `/api/status` shows no active run; PLAN.md stays untracked. The owner reads Turkish; everything written is English.

### 158. A model out of reach does not fail a run

**Status: done.** Merged as `852ccc5` (PR #195; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** When a step's call to the run's own model fails because the model cannot be reached (the
connection broke or timed out, the call took longer than `model_call_timeout_s`, or its server failed with a status that
retrying can get past, such as 500, 503 or 529, after the connector's own tries) and no standby model takes the run
over, the loop waits and asks the same step again: after 10 seconds, then 20 and 40, then every 60, each delay at most a
quarter of the whole wait and never past its end, for `model_wait_s` in `[agent]` (900 seconds by default; 0 does not
wait) from the first failure. The step is not counted again. Each try that fails is a `model_waiting` event (the model,
the error in a few words, the step, the delay and the time the wait ends) and the answer that ends the wait a
`model_back` event (how long it waited); the run's timeline shows one line for the wait, which each try rewrites, and
one for the return. A stop during the wait ends the run at once. A model still out of reach when the wait is over fails
the run, and the result names the wait and the error; a refused request ends the run at once, as does a quota,
rate-limit or key error or a missing key that no standby model takes over. Before, the first such failure after the
connector's tries failed the run. Tests: `tests/smoke/test_model_wait.py` runs a scripted model behind a connection that
fails, with the error the connector raises: twice, after which the run asks the same step again and ends done, with two
`model_waiting` events, one `model_back` and four calls for its two steps; once with a 529, after which it ends done;
always, after which it fails at the end of a wait of two seconds, having asked again at least four times; always with a
stop during a wait of ten minutes, which ends the run in less than three seconds; with a 400, and with a 429 (a status
the connector retries, but a rate limit), each of which fails the run at once. The first four failed on the code of
before, where the first failure ended the run. The run's page was checked in a browser, wide and on a phone, light and
dark, with a run that waited and went on and one that failed at the end of its wait.

**What.** A run whose model cannot be reached for a while (the network drops, its server fails for a time) waits for it
and goes on from the same step, for a time the owner sets, instead of failing; its page shows the wait and the return.

### 159. A stop of the daemon is never a crash

**Status: done.** Merged as `30a4480` (PR #196; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** A wait and a loss of the daemon's way out, each read again in the code first. (1) The way out
waited for a reflection under way (`Scheduler.drain`), whose calls of the review model can take `model_call_timeout_s`
each, past the thirty seconds launchd gives the daemon before it kills it, and the next start then takes the stop for a
crash. `Scheduler.stop`, the first part of the way out, now cancels it: a reflection records nothing until its end, so
the next one reads the same runs again. (2) A step stored its results only once all its calls had ended, so a stop of
the run or of the daemon during a call lost the results of the calls of the step that had ended: the conversation showed
them as interrupted, a resumed run was told only the start of each, and a message that went on in the chat nothing of
them. `execute_calls` now tells the loop of each call that ends, and a step cut by a stop stores their results, in the
order of the calls, before the run ends; a crash still keeps none. The daemon's log holds no stop that launchd had to
kill, so the rest of the way out, where the runs end at their next wait once they are cancelled, keeps no bound of its
own. Found on the way: the README said that a night the daemon slept through is caught up at its start, while the
reflection catches up a night the Mac slept through when it wakes, and a daemon that was off at that time reflects at
the next `reflection_time` on everything since the last reflection; the README says so now. Tests:
`tests/smoke/test_clean_stop.py` cuts, by the daemon's way out, a run whose step writes a file and then runs a command
that waits, while the command runs: the run ends cancelled by the shutdown, the thread holds the write's result and none
for the command, and only the command is left for a resumed run to look at; and it takes the daemon's way out while a
reflection waits for the review model: the way out takes less than ten seconds and records no reflection. Both failed on
the code of before (the thread held no result; the way out waited past ten seconds).

**What.** A stop of the daemon (the service stopped or restarted, a log-out) does not wait for a reflection under way,
whose calls of the model could keep it past the time launchd gives it before it is killed, and a step it cuts keeps the
results of the calls that had ended, so that the run, resumed, does not make them again.

### 160. Pages catch up after a break

**Status: done.** Merged as `4ff0b40` (PR #197; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** Read again in the code first: every page that follows the stream of the lifecycle
(`/api/stream`) read what it shows again only when one of its events came, and the stream replays nothing after a break,
so after the network dropped or the daemon restarted a page kept what it showed before: Activity, Campaigns, Schedules,
the agents and an agent's page, the team, the home's Today strip, and a run's page with its queue. Only the sidebar read
its lists again when the stream was back. `onStreamBack` in `state.js` now tells each page that follows the stream when
the stream is live again after a break, and the page reads again what it shows, the sidebar through it too; a run's page
reads its run again (`reconcile`), its lessons and its questions among it. A page that fails to read again is told like
an event it could not show, and the others still read. The stream was not given a replay from the last event a page had:
some changes send no event at all (a restart closes the runs it finds active), and reading again covers them where a
replay would not. Tests: `tests/smoke/test_catch_up.py` serves a runtime in a throw-away home by a real server that it
takes down and brings back up while the runtime works on, and Chrome shows the pages: the Activity page lists under
Ended today a run that started and ended while the page was away, and a run's page shows in its queue a message queued
while it was away. Both failed on the code of before, where the pages kept what they showed.

**What.** A page whose connection to the daemon broke reads again what it shows once the connection is back, since the
stream of the lifecycle replays nothing and what changed meanwhile may have sent no event at all; a run's page reads its
run again, its lessons and its questions among it, not only its events.

### 161. A chat's queue goes on after a clean restart

**Status: done.** Merged as `2ff66d6` (PR #198; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** Read again in the code first: a run that the daemon's stop cuts off leaves its chat's queue
as it is (the queue is not followed while the daemon stops), but every start of the daemon held every queue
(`hold_every_queue` in `RunManager.recover`), so after a restart or a log-out the owner had to resume the queue as well
as the run: Continue went on with the run, and once the new run had ended done the queue still waited for Resume.
`recover` now holds a chat's queue only when the chat's newest run was not cut off by a shutdown of the daemon: a crash
or a restart that did not wait for the run (the start closes the run as cut off), a failure, the owner's stop, a run
that a process that lives drives, and a run that ended done as the daemon stopped, before its next message could start,
hold it as before. A queue whose run a shutdown cut off waits for that run: once it is resumed (Continue, `dotx resume`,
or on its own with `resume = "safe"`) and the new run ends done, the next message starts. Found on the way, and left as
it was: the API takes a queue on the thread of a delegated run, whose end does not move it on, and deleting the chat of
the run that delegated leaves that queue behind with its hold; a queue whose chat has no run left is held at the start,
as before. Tests: `tests/smoke/test_queue.py` cuts off, by the daemon's way out, a run at work whose chat holds a queued
message, starts the daemon again on the same home, and continues the run: the queue is not held, and once the new run
ends done the message starts as the chat's next run (this failed on the code of before, where the start held the queue);
and a run that a process that is gone left active holds its chat's queue at the start.

**What.** The queue of a chat whose run a shutdown of the daemon cut off is not held when the daemon starts again, so it
goes on once that run, resumed, ends done: a stop of the daemon is not the owner's stop of the chat. A crash still holds
the queues.

### 162. A run whose terminal closed can be resumed

**Status: done.** Merged as `3e33fdd` (PR #199; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** Read again in the code first: `dotx run` (and `resume`, `chat`) ended its run on a closed
terminal (SIGHUP) or SIGTERM as Ctrl-C does, as the owner's stop (`RESULT_STOPPED`), which is never resumed, while a
`dotx run` killed outright left its run active for the daemon's next start to close as cut off, which can be resumed:
the end that kept the run's record clean was the one that lost the run. A closed terminal and SIGTERM now cut the run
off (`RunManager.cut_off`, kept like the runs of an emergency stop): it ends cancelled with a result and an ending of
its own (`process_ended`), `cut_off_by` takes it for cut off, and it can be resumed by hand, by `dotx resume` or
Continue on its page, the resumed run's note telling the model that the dotx command that drove it was told to end. The
daemon never resumes it on its own: `resume = "safe"` takes only runs of the web UI. Ctrl-C stays the owner's stop. The
texts that said that the daemon cut a run off now say what cut it off: the resumed run's note in the timeline and in the
terminal, the chat's history (Resumed where the run above was cut off) and the line above the composer (This run was cut
off while it worked; the run's answer says what cut it off). Tests: `tests/smoke/test_cli_run_end.py` sends a real
SIGHUP, and a real SIGTERM, to a `dotx run` in a child process while its command works: the run ends cut off by the end
of its command, and, resumed by hand in the test's own process, the new run ends done and its note says why the run
before it ended; this failed on the code of before, where the run could not be resumed. Ctrl-C still ends the run
stopped, and it cannot be resumed.

**What.** A run of `dotx run` whose terminal is closed, or that gets SIGTERM, can be resumed, by `dotx resume` or from
its page, as a run cut by a stop of the daemon can; Ctrl-C stays the owner's stop.

## Part 27: find help before the hard way (planned 2026-10-13)

The owner's twenty-sixth word, on 2026-10-13, the one that asked for part 26, also asked why Dot tries every way by
itself instead of looking first at the MCP servers and skills of the Mac it works on, which could make its work easier,
and whether that is needed at all: the aim is a smarter system.

**Status (2026-10-13): planned.** Read in the code first. What exists: the instructions already tell a run to use a
matching skill or MCP tool before it builds something itself, and to prefer the shell and command-line programs, then
APIs and MCP tools, then the web, then AppleScript, and the windows of the desktop last; every skill installed is listed
in the instructions by its name and description, and the `skill` tool reads one; the tools of the configured MCP servers
are in the tool list. What is missing: a run knows only what its instructions list, and nothing tells it what the Mac
itself offers: which applications AppleScript can drive and what their dictionaries say, the skills and MCP servers that
the Mac's other agents have set up, or a way to search all of it for a need. Every skill is listed whatever the goal, so
the instructions grow with each one. The evals run without MCP servers and skills, and nothing measures whether a run
took the easy way.

**The shape of this part (the decisions).** Five items, each a pull request of its own: a run finds the help this Mac
offers before it takes the hard way, with `find_help` over the skills it is offered, the tools of its MCP servers and
the applications that AppleScript can drive (163); the skills and MCP servers of the Mac's other agents are found,
read-only, their secrets never read (164); help found elsewhere is added to Dot only with the owner's yes (165); a run's
instructions list the help that fits its goal, picked by relevance when there is much of it (166); evals show whether a
run takes the easy way (167). The search is by words (BM25) first; meaning (embeddings) can join it with 166. Nothing is
installed or configured without the owner.

### How to start part 27 (the handoff prompt)

> Read ROADMAP.md part 27 and the status table of part 9 (rows 163 to 167). One item at a time, in order; the protocol
> of part 5 (branch, gate, PR, Linear MYP issue when the connector is signed in, squash merge, hash in the table, log
> line) is unchanged. Read each gap again in the code before closing it, give each change a test that fails on the code
> of before, and check a page that changes in a browser, wide and on a phone, light and dark. Read the configuration of
> other agents by names and commands only, never a secret in it (an env value, a header, a token). Never touch the
> owner's data directory except to read it, by the kinds and numbers of what is stored, and to restart the daemon when
> `/api/status` shows no active run; PLAN.md stays untracked. The owner reads Turkish; everything written is English.

### 163. A run finds the help this Mac offers before it takes the hard way

**Status: done.** Merged as `4eb3a6c` (PR #200; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** A new tool, `find_help`, in the core group and in every mode. Given a need in a few plain
words, it searches the skills the run is offered (the learned skills of other agents left out, as in the instructions),
the tools of the MCP servers that the run's mode allows and, when the run can use `apple_script`, the applications that
AppleScript can drive: those whose Info.plist names a scripting dictionary (`OSAScriptingDefinition`) or turns
AppleScript on (`NSAppleScriptEnabled`), in `/Applications`, `/System/Applications` (each with its `Utilities`),
`/System/Library/CoreServices` and `~/Applications`. An application is told by the commands and classes of its
dictionary's own suites, read from its `.sdef` file (at most 2 MB; the suites that many applications share are ranked,
not listed), or as keeping its dictionary in no file of its own, or as having one that could not be read. The items are
ranked by Okapi BM25 over their words (the name counted twice; case, accents, common words and plurals do not matter),
and the best eight that score at least half as well as the best one are listed with how to use each: `skill` with its
name, the MCP tool by its name, or `apple_script` with `tell application`, and `sdef` with the application's path, which
prints the whole dictionary. With nothing found it says what to try next; it says so when applications were not
searched. When the tool is offered, the instructions have a section, Help on this Mac: call `find_help` before a hard
way (writing a script or a program for the work, clicking through an application or a site, trial and error in the
shell), and again once a way has failed twice; the description of `apple_script` points to it. The filter of the learned
skills moved from the loop to `offered_to_run`, which both use. Tests: through the real loop, a scripted run in a
scratch home with a skill installed calls `find_help` and is told of that skill first, with how to use it, and that
applications were not searched (the eval configuration has no desktop); this failed on the code of before, where the
tool was unknown. On the Mac, and on the CI's, Calendar comes first for adding an event to a calendar, with the classes
of its own dictionary. Unit tests rank a fixed set of items and read application bundles made in a temporary folder: own
suites listed and the standard suite not, an application without a dictionary file, one whose dictionary is not XML, one
that is not scriptable.

**What.** A run can ask what this Mac already offers for a need (the skills it is offered, the tools of its MCP servers,
the applications that AppleScript can drive, by their own dictionaries) and is told how to use what fits; its
instructions tell it to ask before it takes a hard way.

### 164. The skills and MCP servers of the Mac's other agents are found

**Status: done.** Merged as `490749a` (PR #201; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** A new module, `dotagent.help.elsewhere`, reads the files of the Mac's other agents without
changing anything: the skills of Claude Code (`~/.claude/skills`), of the plugins installed in Claude Code (from
`~/.claude/plugins/installed_plugins.json`, the `skills/` and `.mcp.json` of each one's `installPath`) and of Codex
(`~/.codex/skills`), and the MCP servers of Claude Code (those for every project, in `~/.claude.json`), Claude Desktop,
Cursor, VS Code (`Code/User/mcp.json`, under `servers`) and Codex (`mcp_servers` in `~/.codex/config.toml`). Only what
names a thing is kept: a skill's name, description and folder; a server's name, its transport and what it reaches, the
base name of the program it starts (the whole command's when it is the path of a file, else its first word's, without a
variable such as VS Code's `${env:HOME}`) or the host of its URL, each only when it is a plain name. A server's
arguments, environment and headers, and the rest of its URL, are never kept, logged or told, not even in the reason it
is left out: a command that starts with a URL or with a variable set before the program, either of which can hold a key,
leaves the server out with why, and an entry that cannot be read is told by the keys at fault. A skill is marked as used
when Dot reads its folder, a server when Dot has one under the name it would give it (a plugin's as `<plugin>-<server>`,
by Dot's own rule). A file that cannot be read (not UTF-8, not of its language, an integer of too many digits, brackets
nested too deep), a skill whose `SKILL.md` Dot cannot use and a server that names no command or URL to use are listed
apart with why, and the rest is still found. A `SKILL.md` whose frontmatter is nested too deep for the YAML reader is
now told as such, for Dot's own skills too, where it used to escape as a RecursionError. `dotx skills list` shows them
after Dot's own, with `?` for any character a terminal would act on; `GET /api/skills/elsewhere` returns them; and the
Skills page of Settings has a section, Found on this Mac, read apart from the learned skills so that a failure there
leaves them on the page: the skills folded by agent, then the MCP servers with their agent and what they reach, then
what was left out. Runs do not see them; item 165 adds one with the owner's yes. Tests: a home made in a temporary
folder with every source, and keys and tokens written in arguments, environments, headers and the user and query of a
URL, gives the skills and servers expected, with the ones Dot uses, and none of the keys anywhere in the result; files
that are not JSON, nested too deep or hold an integer of too many digits, skills without frontmatter or nested too deep,
and servers whose arguments hold a number, whose URL leaves an IPv6 address open or whose command starts with a URL or a
variable are left out with why while the rest is found, and none of their keys comes out. On the versions before a
review, the open address and the deep nesting failed the whole reading and the command forms gave a piece of a key as
the program's name; the tests fail on them. Through the API of a real in-process server whose HOME is a folder made
there, `GET /api/skills/elsewhere` lists a Claude Code skill that Dot reads and a Claude Desktop server, never the key
in its environment; this failed on the code of before, where the route did not exist. On this Mac the reading takes
about a tenth of a second.

**What.** The skills and MCP servers that the Mac's other agents have set up (Claude Code and its plugins, Codex, Claude
Desktop, Cursor, VS Code) are found and shown, read-only: their names, descriptions and what they reach, never a secret
(an argument, an env value, a header, a token).

### 165. Help found elsewhere is added only with the owner's yes

**Status: done.** Merged as `52a7c02` (PR #202; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** Settings › Skills, under Found on this Mac, gives each skill and MCP server that Dot can take
an Add to Dot button and each one added a Remove button; both ask first, in Dot's confirm dialog, and
`PUT /api/skills/elsewhere` (`kind`, `agent`, `name`, `added`) makes the change and returns what is found after it, or a
409 with why. A skill is copied into Dot's skills folder (`<home>/skills/<name>`), its hidden entries left out, with a
hidden marker (`.added-elsewhere.json`) of where it came from, which neither the catalog nor the skill tool counts among
its files; runs are offered it at once. The copy is made in a hidden folder beside the skills, its folders made writable
for the owner (some installers leave theirs read-only), and moved into place once checked again. A copy rather than a
link: what a run may not change is fixed when Dot starts, so a link would have let a run outside `yolo` change a skill
that later runs read, while a copy is inside the protected skills folder at once and keeps to what the owner said yes
to. An MCP server is added as a line of `<home>/added-servers.json`: its agent, its name and a SHA-256 fingerprint of
its entry (command, arguments, environment, URL, headers and transport), nothing it is started with; a run outside
`yolo` may read the record but never change it. At each start the daemon reads the entry from the agent's file and,
while its fingerprint is the recorded one, names it by Dot's rule (lower case, `-` for `_` and spaces, then the rule for
server names) and starts it with the others, its tools offered and approved as an `[[mcp]]` server's. An entry changed
since is left out until the owner removes the server and adds it again: a change to the agent's file never starts on the
owner's earlier yes, and the agents' own files stay theirs to write. Remove works by agent and name, and what was added
that its agent no longer has is listed apart (Added, no longer set up) with Remove. What Dot cannot take says why
instead of a button, already in the list: a skill whose name Dot has or that its skills folder holds, or whose folder
holds a link, something that is neither a file nor a folder, or more than 2000 files or 50 MB; a plugin's server, which
comes with its plugin; a server whose name does not fit Dot's rule or is taken (by `[[mcp]]`, a plugin or another added
server), or that uses a variable its agent fills in (any `${...}` in its command, arguments or URL, or one other than
`${NAME}` in its environment or headers); an added server whose entry changed, or uses such a variable by now, is shown
with why Dot leaves it out when it starts. find_help ranks the skills and servers that can be added with the rest, as
Skill found elsewhere or MCP server found elsewhere, with how to ask the owner to add one (`[skills] elsewhere`, on by
default, off in evals); an answer that lists one counts as untrusted content, since others wrote it, and the run's
instructions say a run asks the owner rather than adding one. `dotx skills list` marks what was added and lists what is
no longer set up. The found list now reads the skills of each agent as Dot reads its own folders, the skill folders of
container folders a few levels down included, where it read one level before. Tests: units add a skill from read-only
folders (the copy without the hidden entries and with the marker, read by the catalog, untouched by a later change of
the original), refuse a name Dot has, a folder holding a link (already in the list) and one over a small limit, remove
the copy alone, and keep, tell apart and remove a copy whose original is gone; a server is recorded with a fingerprint
and none of the keys of its entry, makes another agent's server of the same name refused, is resolved at start with its
arguments and environment, is left out at start and told why in the list once its entry changed, and is told apart and
removed once it is gone. Through the API of a real in-process server, a Codex skill and a Claude Desktop server (the
test's MCP fixture, a key in its environment) are added, the skill is offered at once, a second add is a 409, and a
runtime opened next starts the server under Dot's name for it with the key in its environment, while the copy and the
record are among what a run may not change; once its entry changes in Claude Desktop's file, the next start leaves it
out and the list says why, and once it is gone it is still removed. A run through the real loop calls find_help and is
told of a Claude Code skill to ask the owner for, and the answer counts as untrusted. Each failed on the code before:
without the route (405), without find_help's search of what other agents set up (nothing found), without the record
among what a run may not change (it was a temporary file a run could write), without the fingerprint check (the changed
server started) and without the untrusted mark.

**What.** A skill or an MCP server found elsewhere is added to Dot only when the owner says yes, in Settings; a run that
needs one is told to ask the owner, and nothing is installed or configured without that yes.

### 166. A run's instructions list the help that fits its goal

**Status: done.** Merged as `c3a6b83` (PR #203; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** A run's instructions list at most `listed` skills (`[skills] listed`, 20, at least 1). A run
offered more is listed those that share the most words with its goal and with the goals of the latest earlier runs of
its thread (the query its notes are chosen by), the best fit first, by find_help's BM25 (`help.rank.fitting`, split out
of `rank`, which keeps its cut at half the best score for a need of a few words): unlike find_help, the instructions
keep a skill that shares only some of the goal's words, as a goal can ask for more than one kind of work. A line then
says how many more installed skills fit the goal less well, that find_help searches them all and that skill reads one by
its name; when none shares a word with the goal, the line says so instead, and the skill tool's `name` says a name may
come from find_help. A run offered `listed` skills or fewer is given the same instructions as before. A tool group's
line (the `grouped` surface) names at most 16 of its tools; in a bigger group, those whose names and descriptions share
the most words with the goal now come first, where the first 16 were named before. Not done: meaning (embeddings) next
to the words, so a goal in another language than the skills still lists none of them. Tests: a unit test lists every
skill of a run offered few, whatever the goal; of four with a limit of three, the two that share words with a goal of
two kinds of work, the best fit first, with the line of the two others; and none, with its own line, for a goal that
shares no word. Another names first, in its group's line, the four tools of a twenty-tool MCP server that fit the goal,
and keeps the order of a small group. Through the real loop, a run offered four skills with `listed = 2` is sent
instructions that list the two that fit its goal and say two more are installed. Both failed on the code before: the
run's instructions listed all four, and the line named the first sixteen tools.

**What.** A run's instructions list the skills and tools that fit its goal, picked by relevance when there are many,
instead of every one; the rest stay a `find_help` call away.

### 167. Evals show whether a run takes the easy way

**Status: done.** Merged as `3dc670c` (PR #204; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** A task of the catalog can bring help: skills, written into the skills folder of the attempt's
throw-away home, and MCP servers, added to its run's configuration (the owner's own stay switched off). Its `easy_way`
names the tool of that help, and the skill when that tool is `skill`; an attempt took it when a call of that tool, for
that skill, ran without failing, so a call that did not run (its tool group off, or refused by the policy) does not
count. Three tasks of a new kind, `help`: a memo in a house style that only a skill states (`memo-in-house-style`, the
only way to pass); a quarter's paid orders, which a skill's one command totals (`paid-orders-by-skill`); and the working
days between two dates, which a tool of the evals' own MCP server counts (`working-days-by-mcp`;
`python -m dotagent.evals.tool_server`, a stdio server with one read-only tool). The last two can also be done the hard
way, by reading the files and working it out. An attempt's outcome says whether it took the easy way (`easy_way_taken`;
none for the other tasks and in older reports), and its metrics count the calls of find_help. The score says how many
attempts at such tasks took the easy way and what a pass cost in steps when it did and when it did not, with find_help's
calls; the line of two reports gives the share taken in percentage points, and the comparison table has a column for it.
`dotx eval check` replays the three references through the real loop (the skills read from the attempt's home, the MCP
server started and its tool's answer returned) and reports a reference that does not take its task's easy way; the
catalog's own check reports an easy way that is not one of the task's help. Not done: a task that a scriptable
application makes short, as the evals run without the Mac desktop so that a result does not depend on the Mac's
applications; and a measurement, as no model has played the three tasks yet. Tests: unit tests of the easy way (the
right skill, another skill, an MCP call that did not run and then one that ran), of find_help's count, of the score's
line, difference and column (`-` for an older report), of the catalog's check, and of the working days (32 from 2 March
to 17 April 2026). A smoke test replays the three references through the real loop, each taking its easy way, and a run
that works the orders out itself, which passes without it, and checks that the user's home stays empty. Failed before:
an easy way counted from the call alone counted a call that did not run; with a reference that skips the skill, without
the skills written into the home, or without the server given to the run, `dotx eval check` reported that the reference
does not take the easy way; and with the skills folder taken before the attempt's home is set, the smoke test failed.

**What.** Evals measure whether a run takes the easy way: tasks that a skill, an MCP tool or a scriptable application
makes short, scored by the steps and the channel the run took.

## Part 28: what part 27's report found (planned 2026-10-13)

The owner's twenty-seventh word, on 2026-10-13, after the report of part 27: go on from where the work was left. The
work planned was done, so going on is closing what that report found and left open.

**Status (2026-10-13): planned.** Each gap was read again in the code. The `skill` tool loads every skill installed, so
a run reads a learned skill of another agent by its name, and its refusal of a name it does not know lists every skill
installed, while the instructions and `find_help` leave such skills out (item 94). `find_help` and the skills a run's
instructions list (item 166) are ranked by words alone: a goal in Turkish shares no word with a skill described in
English, so `find_help` finds nothing for it, and a run offered more than twenty skills has none of them listed; part 27
said meaning could join the words, and it did not. A chat's queue (item 148) refuses the chat of a campaign but takes
the thread of a delegated run through the API (its page has no composer): the delegated run's end leaves its queue
alone, so a message queued there never starts, and with no run at work there it starts a run of its own on the helper's
thread; deleting the chat of the run that delegated deletes the helper's thread and leaves its queue. The text of a
desktop window is sized when Dot starts, from the setting of the tool results, while the text of a page follows the
run's model window, so on a model with a small window the executor cuts the middle out of a window's text. Only the
daemon closes the runs of a process that is gone, and only when it starts: a `dotx` command that is killed, or quit with
a second Ctrl-C before its run's end is written, leaves the run at work on every page until the daemon starts again,
which then says that the daemon stopped. A test of the MCP hub fails when it runs alone, since the workspace it needs is
made by the fixture of another test, and some of the README's prose is wider than 120 columns.

**The shape of this part (the decisions).** Six items, each a pull request of its own, the most important first: a run
reads only the skills it is offered (168); help is found by meaning as well as by words, with the embeddings the notes
already use (169); a delegated run's thread takes no queue (170); the text of a desktop window follows the run's model
window (171); a `dotx` command that dies does not leave its run at work (172); every smoke test passes alone, and the
README keeps its width (173). Not in this part: a bound on the whole of the daemon's stop (no stop has been cut short in
the owner's logs, and item 159 bounded the part that could take minutes); versions of notes, resuming by default (an
eval on a live model must show first that it helps) and an eval task that a scriptable application makes short (the
evals run without the desktop).

### 168. A run reads only the skills it is offered

**Status: done.** Merged as `f605def` (PR #206; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** The `skill` tool reads a skill only from those the run is offered (`offered_to_run`, the
filter of the instructions and of `find_help`): a learned skill of another agent that is not shared is not read by its
name, and a name the run is not offered is refused with the words that no skill offered to the run is called so, and the
names of only those that are. The tool's name (`SKILL_TOOL`) moved next to `SKILL_FILE` in `skills/types.py`, so that
the module of the learned skills, which counts the runs that read them, no longer imports the tool. Tests:
`tests/smoke/test_skills_runtime.py` writes a learned skill of an agent into a scratch home; a run of that agent reads
it, a run of Dot is refused without its steps, and the names a refusal lists leave it out. On the code of before, Dot's
run read the agent's skill whole.

**What.** A run reads only the skills it is offered: the `skill` tool leaves out what the instructions and `find_help`
leave out, and a refusal names only the skills the run is offered.

### 169. Help is found by meaning as well as by words

**Status: done.** Merged as `5c96b14` (PR #207; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** With the memory's embeddings on (`[memory] embed_enabled`, the default; bge-m3 on the local
Ollama server reads Turkish as well as English), `find_help` ranks the help it searches by meaning as well as by words:
the items whose embedding is at least `[memory] min_similarity` (0.50) close to the need's, the closest first, are fused
with those that share its words (BM25, the half-the-best floor kept) by reciprocal rank fusion, as the notes are, and
the best eight are listed. A run offered more skills than `[skills] listed` (20) is given those that fit its goal best
the same way. The embedding of each text that help is ranked by is made once and kept while Dot runs (`help/meaning.py`,
`HelpVectors` on the runtime, at most 4096 texts): embedding 150 of them took bge-m3 about seven seconds on this Mac,
one need some 30 ms. When the embedding service fails, `find_help` lists what the words found and says that finding help
by meaning failed (as it says when what other agents set up could not be searched), and logs `help_meaning_failed`; the
skills of a run's instructions, when they must be picked, fail the run's start instead, as its notes do. With the
embeddings off (and in the evals), by words as before. A big tool group's line still names the tools that share the
goal's words first. The instructions' line for a run none of whose skills fits now says that none clearly fits its goal,
not that none shares a word with it. Tests: unit tests rank items and list skills with a ranking by meaning (a need and
a goal in Turkish that share no word find the item close to them, and an item both rankings hold comes first), and check
that each text is embedded once and that the texts kept are bounded. Through the real loop with bge-m3 (skipped where it
is not installed, as in the CI), a run offered four skills with two listed and a goal in Turkish is listed the report's
skill first, and its `find_help` call with a need in Turkish is told of that skill first; on the code of before, none
was listed and nothing was found. With the embedding service out of reach, a run's `find_help` call is told of the skill
its words find, and that finding help by meaning failed. Measured with bge-m3 on texts made for the test: a Turkish need
comes 0.52 to 0.72 close to the English skill made for it, which comes first; a related one can pass 0.50 too (release
notes, at 0.54, for a report written from notes), and a need unrelated to every skill stays below 0.40.

**What.** `find_help` and the skills a run's instructions list are ranked by meaning as well as by words, with the
embeddings the notes use (bge-m3 runs on this Mac and reads Turkish as well as English), so a goal in one language finds
help described in another; with the embeddings off, by words as before.

### 170. A delegated run's thread takes no queue

**Status: done.** Merged as `336e03f` (PR #208; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** A message queued on the thread of a delegated run (`POST /api/threads/{id}/queue` where the
thread's newest run has a parent) is refused with 409, as one on the chat of a campaign is: that thread is no chat, its
page has no composer, and the run that delegated decides what follows. Before, the API took it, and the delegated run's
end left the queue alone, so the message never started, or, with no run at work there, it started a run of its own on
the helper's thread. Deleting a chat now deletes the queue and the hold of the threads of the runs it delegated, along
with those threads, unless a run of their own remains there. Tests: in `tests/smoke/test_queue.py`, the thread of a
delegated run refuses a message, and nothing waits or starts there; in `tests/smoke/test_server.py`, deleting a chat
leaves no queue on the deleted thread of the run it delegated, and keeps the queue of a grandchild's thread that holds a
run of its own. On the code of before, the message was taken, and the queue of the deleted thread stayed.

**What.** The thread of a delegated run takes no queue, as the chat of a campaign takes none, and deleting a chat
deletes the queues of the threads of the runs it delegated.

### 171. The text of a desktop window follows the run's model window

**Status: done.** Merged as `047d0e1` (PR #209; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** The most text of an application window a desktop result carries is now worked out per call
from the run's own tool output budget (`ctx.output_chars`, which a model with a small window lowers), as the text of a
page already was: `snapshot_budget(config, output_chars)` keeps 3500 characters for the rest of the result, never less
than half of it, and never more than `[desktop] snapshot_max_chars`. `desktop_snapshot`, `desktop_open_app` and
`desktop_act` (its window after the batch) hand it to the desktop session with the view they ask for
(`ViewRequest.max_chars`). Before, the session was built once with the budget of the configured `tool_output_chars`
(8500 characters), so a run whose model has a window of 16 000 tokens, whose results carry 2000, got about 8400
characters of window text, and the executor cut out their middle; now it gets 1000, with the rows left out counted.
`dotx desktop snapshot` keeps the configured budget. The README's line on the budget (the text of a page or an
application window takes what is left next to the rest of the result) now holds for the desktop too. Tests: a unit test
renders a window of 600 rows for such a run, and the whole of it fits in one of its results; a probe on the code of
before rendered 8394 characters for a result of 2000. The desktop smoke tests (`desktop`-marked, run only on a Mac set
up for them) pass the budget of a view; they were collected, not run.

**What.** The text of a desktop window follows the run's model window, as the text of a page does, so the executor never
cuts it in the middle.

### 172. A dotx command that dies does not leave its run at work

**Status: done.** Merged as `bbb40bc` (PR #210; no Linear issue, the Linear connector was signed out).

**As built (2026-10-13).** Every 30 seconds while it runs, the daemon closes the runs that a `dotx` command (`run`,
`resume`, `chat`) left active when its process ended without recording their end, killed or crashed: their owner's lock
is no longer held (`RunManager.close_runs_of_dead_commands`, `Store.close_runs_of`). Such a run fails with a result that
names the command (`RESULT_COMMAND_DIED`, the ending `process_died`, "cut off when its dotx command died"), finished at
its last sign of life, and its `run_finished` event is stored in the same write, then told to the pages that follow it.
Its pending approvals expire ("its dotx command died"), and the queue of its chat is held until the owner resumes it, as
after any end that is not done. The files of gone owners go at each check, those of commands that ended well too, which
before stayed until the daemon's next start. A check that fails on the store or on those files is logged, and the next
one goes on. The run can be resumed by hand, and the resumed run is told that the command that drove it died (in its
first message, on its page and in the terminal); like any run of the command line, the daemon never resumes it on its
own. Before, such a run stayed at work until the daemon's next start, which closed it as cut off by the daemon ("daemon
stopped while the run was active"); that start still closes what any gone process left, since it cannot tell a command's
runs from those of the daemon before it. A second Ctrl-C now quits once the stop that the first one asked for is
recorded, five seconds at most, and says so when it is not (the daemon then closes the run). Before, it closed the
runtime without waiting, and the stop was written only when the run's end came before the store closed, last: a test
that presses Ctrl-C twice saw the run end stopped on the code of before as after, so that wait makes certain what was
likely. Tests: in `tests/smoke/test_cli_run_end.py`, a `dotx run` in a child process is killed with SIGKILL while its
command works: its run is left at work, the daemon's check closes it as `process_died`, stores and tells `run_finished`,
holds the queue of its chat and clears the dead command's owner file, and the run resumed by hand is told that its
command died. The code of before had no such check. Not done: a campaign whose first session's command died plans its
next session at the daemon's next start, as before.

**What.** The run of a `dotx` command that dies is closed while the daemon runs, not at its next start, and is said to
be cut off by its command's end rather than by the daemon; a second Ctrl-C still writes the stop that the first one
asked for.
